title: Marathon Oil Co. v. EPA (1977)
summary: The Ninth Circuit required formal adjudicatory procedure for individual discharge permits and remanded because the agency used material outside the hearing record.

sections.Parties: Oil companies operating offshore platforms and onshore treatment facilities in Cook Inlet, Alaska, petitioned for review of EPA discharge permits. The EPA defended the effluent limits and the procedures used to set them.
sections.Material Facts: The permits regulated deck drainage, water produced with oil and gas, and sanitary wastes. The companies argued that the limits exceeded what the best practicable control technology could achieve. The governing statute authorized permits after an opportunity for public hearing. EPA gave adjudicatory hearings under its regulations but denied that all APA formal-hearing requirements applied. In deciding the permits, the Administrator apparently used a new year of data and an internal statistical memorandum not included in the hearing record.
sections.Procedural History: The Ninth Circuit considered consolidated petitions challenging both substantive limits and procedure. It ordered a limited remand, including new hearings at which petitioners could address the previously undisclosed data and memorandum. Judge Wallace agreed with the majority’s statutory interpretation but dissented from its disposition of the constitutional challenge. The substantive analysis and much of the constitutional discussion are omitted by the casebook.
sections.Issue: Does a statutory opportunity for public hearing on individual pollution-discharge permits require APA §§ 554, 556, and 557 despite omission of the phrase on the record? If so, did use of undisclosed material violate that framework?
sections.Holding: The formal-hearing provisions applied to these permits. The statutory words need not be a verbal formula when the proceeding’s quasi-judicial character and statutory context support an on-the-record hearing. Reliance on material outside the record required a limited remand. The court rejected the presented due-process objection to review by the Regional Administrator who had issued the draft permits.
sections.Reasoning: The majority distinguished industry-wide effluent policy from deciding what limits are practicable for particular sources. Individual permits turned on sharply disputed facts and fit both the APA’s classification of licensing and its traditional concern with quasi-judicial proceedings. Congress’s requirement of a hearing supported a presumption of formal safeguards absent contrary intent; omission of the precise phrase on the record did not defeat that conclusion. Section 556(e) then confined the decision to the record and required a chance to address additional material. The remand created that opportunity and did not establish the companies’ preferred discharge limits. The following notes explain that other circuits later used Chevron deference differently and that Loper Bright destabilizes that later rationale; this 1977 decision should therefore be read as an assigned historical approach rather than an uncontested nationwide present-day rule.

topics.lrs-o-hearing-trigger: For permit adjudication the court treated the hearing requirement as invoking formal safeguards, distinguishing the rulemaking setting in Florida East Coast.
topics.lrs-o-administrative-evidence: The remand required an opportunity to challenge new data and the Liberson memorandum outside the hearing record.
topics.lrs-o-apa-classification: The decision turns on classifying individual permit decisions as adjudication subject to §§ 554, 556 and 557.
